274495776_8970fb4f.text: The thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN), a thin shell of GABAergic neurons positioned between the thalamus and cortex, receives its excitatory drive from the collateral projections of both thalamocortical and corticothalamic neurons and sends its inhibitory input to the thalamus to modulate thalamic activity

274495776_ea6ec372.text: .Our recent single-cell RNA sequencing analysis of the TRN demonstrated two neuronal populations defined by a transcriptomic gradient of over 100 differentially expressed genes. SPP1 and ECEL1 are the two genes most differentially expressed by the two transcriptional poles of this gradient. SPP1-expressing (Spp1+) and ECEL1-expressing (Ecel1+) neurons have distinct anatomical localization, efferent connectivity, electrophysiological profiles, and opposing functions in regulating sleep rhythms. (Li et al., 2020) Specifically, Spp1+ neurons are located in the central core of the TRN, exhibit high bursting activity, project to first-order (FO) thalamic nuclei, and contribute to sleep spindle generation and delta rhythm power during slow-wave sleep. Conversely, Ecel1+ neurons, found in the bordering shell of the TRN, exhibit low bursting activity, project to higher-order (HO) thalamic nuclei, and antagonize sleep spindle duration. In addition to distinct outputs to thalamic nuclei, the TRN also receives abundant inputs from cortical, thalamic, and other subcortical regions.
